title: The effect of dietary emulsifiers and thickeners on intestinal barrier function and its response to acute stress in healthy adult humans: A randomised controlled feeding study
authors: Fitzpatrick JA, Gibson PR, Taylor KM, Halmos EP
followUp: 28 days on each diet with at least 3 weeks of washout
funder: JAF is a recipient of the Crohn's and Colitis Australia PhD Scholarship. EPH was supported through research grants from the National Health & Medical Research Council Investigator Grant and Crohn's & Colitis Foundation Litwin Pioneers Program. The study was supported by a grant from the Eva and Tom Breuer Foundation.
authorConflicts: PRG and EPH declared consultancies, shareholdings, honoraria or research grants from companies including Atmo Biosciences, Mindset Health, Dr Falk Pharma, Ferring, Janssen, AbbVie and Takeda; the other authors declared none.
result: Single-blinded cross-over feeding trial of high- against low-emulsifier diets, both with all food provided. Unstressed median 2 h urinary lactulose:rhamnose ratio 0.030 (IQR 0.018 to 0.042) on the high-emulsifier diet against 0.042 (0.029 to 0.078) on the low-emulsifier diet (P = 0.04), with lower lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (P = 0.026) and no difference in epithelial injury or inflammation markers. After intravenous corticotrophin-releasing hormone the ratio rose by 89% on the high-emulsifier diet (P = 0.004) and fell by 39% on the low-emulsifier diet (P = 0.009), the two differing (P = 0.001).
